Drama. The literary form composed of dialogue and action designed for live performance before an audience, encompassing tragedy, comedy, and all genres in between. Distinguished from narrative literature by its direct representation of character and action through performers on stage, drama has been a central mode of human storytelling since ancient Greece and remains vital to culture. The form uniquely engages an audience through immediate, physical presence—the unfolding of events in real time, the actor's body and voice, the architecture of the theatre space itself. Drama is structured around dialogue; the audience experiences the story through what characters say and do, rather than through narration or description. Classical dramatic structure, codified by Aristotle and refined over centuries, involves exposition, rising action, climax, and resolution, a framework that remains influential. Major genres include tragedy, ending in disaster; comedy, ending in resolution and celebration; and variations like tragicomedy, farce, and melodrama. Different eras transformed the form's conventions and possibilities. Greek drama, Elizabethan drama particularly Shakespeare, French neoclassical drama, and modern and contemporary drama each shaped what theatre could do. In the modern era, drama has exploded beyond the proscenium stage to include film, television, radio, and experimental performance, yet the core elements of character, dialogue, and conflict remain central. Playwrights like Anton Chekhov revolutionized drama by eliminating traditional climactic action in favor of psychological subtlety and the emotional texture of ordinary life. The highest form of drama in classical aesthetics, tragedy centres on the fall of noble figures and produces catharsis. Its counterpart, comedy, centres on human folly, mistakes, and resolution through wit and recognition. Greek tragedy established the foundational conventions of unity, action, and moral seriousness that influenced all subsequent drama. The Elizabethan era witnessed drama reach extraordinary heights in the hands of William Shakespeare and his contemporaries. Drama exists fully only in performance, making the embodied realization of dramatic text essential to the form itself.
